newsitem.title: USA: U.S.-Canada salmon talks to resume June 18.
newsitem.headline: U.S.-Canada salmon talks to resume June 18.

text.p: The United States and Canada will resume talks on Wednesday in a dispute over how to divide the Pacific salmon catch, a month after discussions collapsed in acrimony, the U.S. State Department announced on Friday.

The Canadians walked out of the talks on May 21 when a U.S. negotiator said she was not authorised to offer a specific catch reduction on Fraser River sockeye. The two countries have squabbled for years over how to divide the salmon catch in the Pacific Northwest and several attempts at a settlement have failed.
The latest round of talks fell apart at the same time Alaskan officials reported a huge catch in the opening day of their salmon fishing season.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns announced the resumption of talks, to take place in Vancouver, in a brief written statement. "The U.S. side looks forward to productive discussions," he wrote.

Canada, concerned about overfishing by U.S. boats as salmon head through Alaskan waters into Canadian waters to breed, seized four American fishing vessels after the breakdown of the talks last month.

The boats were released after their skippers paid small fines, but the United States said the action poisoned the atmosphere for discussions. Pressure has mounted for a deal before this year's salmon run, which will begin shortly.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy have been in touch several times in a bid to re-start the talks.
In May, Alaska Governor Tony Knowles blamed Canadian politics for shelving the talks. Prime Minister Jean Chretien retained control of Parliament in national elections June 2.
